body: You don't need to copy data here, just have two pointers for prev and curr and swap them. Or swap a couple of indices.

I wouldn't try this, it could cause a rendering server sync.
Either cache locally, or you could just ignore the AABBs as the culling is pretty approximate anyway.
Vector uses copy-on-write, I think the copy is not expensive.
The copy is cheap when the mesh is very simple, but it becomes more and more expensive as the mesh is more detailed.

I didn't notice it was using `Vector`.

Might be worth double checking it's not doing any extra allocation / deallocation as a result, @Ivorforce is the guy to ask here. `unref` seems to call `Memory::free_static`..

If `buffer_prev` is `Vector`, we don't want to be calling `ptrw()` in a tight loop as it invokes the COW machinery.
Probably better to get raw pointers outside the loop?
`Vector` copying is cheap as long as both copies aren't modified (or accidentally trigger CoW, which does happen...). Otherwise, it's just as expensive as a regular copy.

To me it still sounds with the potential pitfalls it might be a good idea to use the e.g. two pointers and SWAP approach to be a bit safer.

I'm not sure there's anything to gain using the operator = here, and a lot to potentially go wrong.

~if we don't use operator =, we need to always copy the buffer to buffer_prev, which is unnecessary if the buffer doesn't change.~ Swapping pointers should be better. I also think there be unnecessary allocation here.

This both allocates everytime, and copies everytime.
Better to pre-allocate an interpolated buffer.

Also, when physics interpolation is off, you can avoid the copy and just update the data straight from the `current_buffer`.

This means BTW, that you may still be better off keeping the buffers as `Vector` rather than `LocalVector`. It depends whether the rendering server creates a copy anyway via COW (this might need investigation or testing).

You can precalculate this stride difference outside the loop.
The optimizer may be able to do this for you, but worth testing (and it won't in debug).
`Vector` and `LocalVector` support move semantics, so I think we can swap them directly.

Oh I forgot we added move semantics.
I would still use the pointers, better to make it explicit with stuff like this imo.

It's not clear to the reader what it is doing currently, and is dependent on the behaviour of the container.

Might be safer to have this condition be if the size is not equal, just in case the editor has changed the size of the soft body, or something like that?

The `resize` function likely does this redundant check for us, but not a lot of harm in doing this explicitly as it should get optimized out.

No need to do this if physics interpolation is off.
We want things to be zero cost (or close to) for projects not using physics interpolation, both in terms of processing and memory use.

Probably worth pre-calculating the strides in units, just to make it faster in debug in this tight loop.
I don't think it's less clear, especially if you call it something like `stride_units` and `normal_stride_units`.
Do we need to be using `process_internal` and `physics_process_internal` when physics interpolation is off?

IMO it is clearer to use move semantics, ~and there is already a precedent:~

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/99f5a3d665cfcc517b0b4b55d8668c2116effb69/servers/rendering/storage/mesh_storage.cpp#L368

Edit: alright, it uses pointers 😅
It should be initialized only once. Setting mesh will clear the buffers each time.
`physics_process` is always required, while `process` may be not. I have modified to upload mesh within `process` only when physics interpolation is on.

Existing implementation doesn't rely on `physics_process()` though when physics interpolation is OFF, updates seem handled by the physics already.

Usually it can be a good idea to avoid adding `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS` unless necessary, as the machinery isn't all that efficient, and it allows the physics to e.g. sleep when the soft body is no longer moving, or turn off when required.

It's fine to make this dependency when physics interpolation is ON, but am a little uneasy about adding unnecessary restriction when physics interpolation is OFF.

Golden rule I'm trying to go by as we roll out FTI, is not to make existing stuff slower (and hopefully not make existing code get over-complicated by the addition). It's not fair on users and maintainers who _aren't_ using physics interpolation is my thinking.

Maybe like keeping the old `commit_changes()` (that is a NOOP when physics interpolation is on) and adding a new one for physics interpolation, something like that.

Other than that, this is looking great. :+1:
I don't know why GitHub didn't mark the changes discussed here as outdated. I have disabled `process` when physical interpolation is off. It shouldn't be slower than before.

It did, what I am questioning is whether it should have to use `INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS` _at all_ when physics interpolation is off, the current code doesn't require this notification.

_(sorry my fault I typed the wrong notification in previous post, have now corrected.)_
The current code used `frame_pre_draw` signal, which is similar to `process` I think. We use notifications in most places, is there any reasons to use `frame_pre_draw` instead of `physics_process`?

I hadn't noticed that .. and was assuming it was being triggered entirely from the physics.

But now you have mentioned it :grin: :

* `frame_pre_draw` will occur before the _frame_
* `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS` occurs before the physics tick

This means with higher tick rate than frame rate, it will be updating the soft mesh more than before (and more than necessary) I think?

The other thing is that `frame_pre_draw` occurs at a different point than `INTERNAL_PROCESS` (pre-empting if you wondering about changing it to that). `INTERNAL_PROCESS` happens afaik before `_process()` so users can still move an Object during the frame process, and with the old system, it will still be reflected on that frame.

If you changed it from `PHYSICS_PROCESS` to `PROCESS` this behaviour would change. That's a sacrifice that's fine for physics interpolation but we don't want to change existing behaviour.

Also could be important in the light of #86808 (which I just saw this morning). If indeed the physics needs a sync then where this is called could be important.
